assessment.title: Shakespeare and the 19th-century novel
assessment.content: Section A: one question on a chosen Shakespeare play. Section B: one question on a chosen 19th-century novel.
assessment.format: Each question gives an extract to analyse in detail, then asks about the text as a whole. Section A carries 30 marks (AO1, AO2, AO3) plus 4 marks for AO4; Section B carries 30 marks.

assessment.title: Modern texts and poetry
assessment.content: Section A: modern prose or drama. Section B: Poems Past and Present anthology cluster. Section C: unseen poetry.
assessment.format: Section A: one essay from a choice of two. Section B: one comparative question on a printed named poem and one other poem from the studied cluster. Section C: one question on an unseen poem and one comparing it with a second unseen poem.

nonExam: None. Closed book: texts are not allowed in the exam; any extract or poem needed is printed on the paper.

aos.desc: Read, understand and respond to texts: maintain a critical style, develop an informed personal response, use textual references including quotations.
Analyse the language, form and structure used by a writer to create meanings and effects, using relevant subject terminology.
Show understanding of the relationships between texts and the contexts in which they were written.
Use a range of vocabulary and sentence structures for clarity, purpose and effect, with accurate spelling and punctuation.

units.title: Paper 1 Section A: Shakespeare (choose one play)
points: One question on the play studied; the paper offers a question on each of the six plays.
Students first write in detail about a printed extract, then about the play as a whole.
Marks: 30 for AO1, AO2 and AO3 (about 12, 12 and 6) plus 4 for AO4 on this section only (per specimen).
Context (AO3) is credited where it is linked to the question, not as a separate block.
Extract questions focus on one theme or character, such as power, ambition or attitudes.

units.title: Shakespeare options listed by AQA
points: Macbeth.
Romeo and Juliet.
The Tempest.
The Merchant of Venice.
Much Ado About Nothing.
Julius Caesar.

units.title: SCHOOL CHOICE: Macbeth (Shakespeare, Section A)
points: The school teaches Macbeth, one of the six plays AQA allows.
Taught in Year 11: context and the witches, then tyranny, guilt and downfall.
Exam skill: respond to a printed extract, then range across the whole play.
Theme work linked to the Section A question style: power, ambition, kingship, conscience.
Section A response writing is the final taught unit.

units.title: Paper 1 Section B: the 19th-century novel (choose one)
points: One question on the novel studied; the paper offers a question on each of the seven novels.
Same structure as Section A: detailed extract analysis, then the text as a whole.
30 marks across AO1, AO2 and AO3; AO4 is not separately credited in Section B (per specimen).
Context credit relates to Victorian or Regency society as it bears on the question.
Extract questions focus on a character, relationship or idea, such as outsiders or class.

units.title: 19th-century novel options listed by AQA
points: The Strange Case of Dr Jekyll and Mr Hyde (Robert Louis Stevenson).
A Christmas Carol (Charles Dickens).
Great Expectations (Charles Dickens, 1867).
Jane Eyre (Charlotte Bronte).
Frankenstein (Mary Shelley, 1831 edition).
Pride and Prejudice (Jane Austen).
The Sign of Four (Sir Arthur Conan Doyle).

units.title: SCHOOL CHOICE: A Christmas Carol (19th-century novel, Section B)
points: The school teaches A Christmas Carol, one of the seven novels AQA allows.
Taught in Year 10: Victorian context and Stave 1, then the Spirits and redemption.
Exam skill: analyse an extract, then use the rest of the novella in the answer.
Themes studied include social responsibility, poverty, redemption and being an outsider.
A dedicated lesson covers writing the exam response.

units.title: Paper 2 Section A: Modern prose or drama text (choose one)
points: One essay question, chosen from a choice of two, on the text studied.
No printed extract: the answer draws on knowledge of the whole text.
Assessed for AO1, AO2 and AO3, with AO4 credited on the written accuracy of this essay.
Context (AO3) is credited when it supports the argument.

units.title: Modern text options listed by AQA
points: Drama: An Inspector Calls, Blood Brothers (musical version), DNA, A Taste of Honey.
Drama, newer: Princess and the Hustler, Leave Taking (first exam 2025).
Drama, last exam 2024: The History Boys, The Curious Incident of the Dog in the Night-Time (play script).
Prose: Lord of the Flies, Animal Farm, Anita and Me, Pigeon English, AQA Anthology: Telling Tales.
Prose, newer: My Name is Leon (first exam 2025).
Prose, last exam 2024: Never Let Me Go.

units.title: Paper 2 Section B: Poetry, Poems Past and Present (one cluster)
points: Study one cluster of 15 poems, written between 1789 and the present day.
Clusters: Love and Relationships; Power and Conflict; Worlds and Lives (first exam 2025).
One comparative question: a named poem printed on the paper and one other poem from the cluster.
The second poem is chosen from memory, so all 15 must be known well.
Compare ideas, methods and context across the two poems.

units.title: Paper 2 Section C: Unseen poetry
points: Two printed poems the student has not studied.
One question on the first poem, then one comparing it with the second.
Students compare content, theme, structure and language.
Wide reading of poetry is expected as preparation; no poems are prescribed.

units.title: SCHOOL CHOICE: Paper 2 texts and poetry cluster not yet recorded
points: Modern text, anthology cluster and unseen poetry lessons are not in the school's Year 10 or 11 material.
The school's current lessons cover Paper 1 only (A Christmas Carol and Macbeth).
Year 8 War poetry and Year 9 Of Mice and Men are bridge units, not AQA set texts.

commandWords.word: Starting with this extract, explain how...
commandWords.meaning: Paper 1 stem pattern (paraphrased from specimen): analyse the printed extract first, then widen to the whole text.
Paper 1 stem pattern: show how the writer presents the named character, idea or relationship, in the extract and across the text.
Where used, give a supported judgement on a statement about a character or theme.
Paper 2 Section B pattern: compare the named poem with another from the cluster, covering ideas and methods.

commandWords.word: In this poem, how does the poet present...
commandWords.meaning: Paper 2 Section C question on the first unseen poem: analyse methods and ideas.

commandWords.word: In both poems, how is ... presented?
commandWords.meaning: Paper 2 Section C comparison question across the two unseen poems.

skills: Close analysis of an extract, then relating it to the whole text.
Using short, precise quotations to support an argument.
Analysing language, form and structure with subject terminology.
Linking writers' ideas to context without bolting on facts.
Writing a sustained, conceptual essay with an argument.
Comparing two poems on ideas and methods.
Responding to an unseen poem with confidence.
Accurate spelling, punctuation and varied sentences (AO4).
Planning and timing an extended response in a closed-book exam.

prerequisites.from: KS3 Shakespeare study (National Curriculum requires two plays across KS3)
KS3 reading of pre-1914 prose; Year 7 novel study
Year 9 Of Mice and Men: context, character, theme essay
Year 8 War poetry: context, language, comparison
Year 5 poetry (The Eagle) and Year 8 poem analysis
English Language Paper 1 Q2 and Q3 (language and structure)

links.topic: Victorian society: poverty, the Poor Law, industrial Britain
links.how: History gives the Victorian social picture; Literature uses it as AO3 context for the novel.

links.topic: Jacobean England: kingship, James I, the Gunpowder Plot
links.how: History explains beliefs about monarchy; Literature uses them for Shakespeare's context.

links.topic: 20th-century Britain: class and the world wars
links.how: History supplies the period background for modern texts such as An Inspector Calls.

links.topic: Language and structure analysis (AO2) and extended writing
links.how: Language trains the analytical method; Literature applies it to set texts.

links.topic: Scientific ambition and ethics in Frankenstein and Jekyll and Hyde
links.how: Science supplies the ideas of experiment and consequence; Literature analyses how writers present them.

links.topic: Responsibility, relationships and conflict in modern texts and poetry
links.how: PSHE explores the issues; Literature studies how writers present them.

links.topic: Place, environment and nature in poems (Worlds and Lives, Power and Conflict)
links.how: Geography provides place knowledge; Literature analyses poets' response to landscape.

links.topic: Charity, justice and repentance as moral themes in A Christmas Carol
links.how: Islamic Studies gives ethical vocabulary for discussion; Literature stays focused on the writer's methods.

links.topic: Visual imagery and period illustration for Victorian and Gothic texts
links.how: Art analyses visual methods; Literature applies the idea of imagery to language.

contextNote: AO3 requires understanding of the contexts in which each text was written and received. Teach historical, social and literary contexts accurately and link them to the writer's choices; context is credited when it supports the response to the question.
